Avoid passing the intended answer, suspected bug, intended fix, or your prior conclusions unless the validation explicitly requires them.\r\n\r\n### Anatomy of a Skill\r\n\r\nEvery skill consists of a required SKILL.md file and optional bundled resources:\r\n\r\n```\r\nskill-name/\r\nΓö£ΓöÇΓöÇ SKILL.md (required)\r\nΓöé   Γö£ΓöÇΓöÇ YAML frontmatter metadata (required)\r\nΓöé   Γöé   Γö£ΓöÇΓöÇ name: (required)\r\nΓöé   Γöé   ΓööΓöÇΓöÇ description: (required)\r\nΓöé   ΓööΓöÇΓöÇ Markdown instructions (required)\r\nΓö£ΓöÇΓöÇ agents/ (recommended)\r\nΓöé   ΓööΓöÇΓöÇ openai.yaml - UI metadata for skill lists and chips\r\nΓööΓöÇΓöÇ Bundled Resources (optional)\r\n    Γö£ΓöÇΓöÇ scripts/          - Executable code (Python/Bash/etc.)\r\n    Γö£ΓöÇΓöÇ references/       - Documentation intended to be loaded into context as needed\r\n    ΓööΓöÇΓöÇ assets/           - Files used in output (templates, icons, fonts, etc.)\r\n```\r\n\r\n#### SKILL.md (required)\r\n\r\nEvery SKILL.md consists of:\r\n\r\n- **Frontmatter** (YAML): Contains `name` and `description` fields. These are the only fields that Codex reads to determine when the skill gets used, thus it is very important to be clear and comprehensive in describing what the skill is, and when it should be used.\r\n- **Body** (Markdown): Instructions and guidance for using the skill. Only loaded AFTER the skill triggers (if at all).\r\n\r\n#### Agents metadata (recommended)\r\n\r\n- UI-facing metadata for skill lists and chips\r\n- Read references/openai_yaml.md before generating values and follow its descriptions and constraints\r\n- Create: human-facing `display_name`, `short_description`, and `default_prompt` by reading the skill\r\n- Generate deterministically by passing the values as `--interface key=value` to `scripts/generate_openai_yaml.py` or `scripts/init_skill.py`\r\n- On updates: validate `agents/openai.yaml` still matches SKILL.md; regenerate if stale\r\n- Only include other optional interface fields (icons, brand color) if explicitly provided\r\n- See references/openai_yaml.md for field definitions and examples\r\n\r\n#### Bundled Resources (optional)\r\n\r\n##### Scripts (`scripts/`)\r\n\r\nExecutable code (Python/Bash/etc.) for tasks that require deterministic reliability or are repeatedly rewritten.\r\n\r\n- **When to include**: When the same code is being rewritten repeatedly or deterministic reliability is needed\r\n- **Example**: `scripts/rotate_pdf.py` for PDF rotation tasks\r\n- **Benefits**: Token efficient, deterministic, may be executed without loading into context\r\n- **Note**: Scripts may still need to be read by Codex for patching or environment-specific adjustments\r\n\r\n##### References (`references/`)\r\n\r\nDocumentation and reference material intended to be loaded as needed into context to inform Codex's process and thinking.\r\n\r\n- **When to include**: For documentation that Codex should reference while working\r\n- **Examples**: `references/finance.md` for financial schemas, `references/mnda.md` for company NDA template, `references/policies.md` for company policies, `references/api_docs.md` for API specifications\r\n- **Use cases**: Database schemas, API documentation, domain knowledge, company policies, detailed workflow guides\r\n- **Benefits**: Keeps SKILL.md lean, loaded only when Codex determines it's needed\r\n- **Best practice**: If files are large (>10k words), include grep search patterns in SKILL.md\r\n- **Avoid duplication**: Information should live in either SKILL.md or references files, not both. Prefer references files for detailed information unless it's truly core to the skillΓÇöthis keeps SKILL.md lean while making information discoverable without hogging the context window. Keep only essential procedural instructions and workflow guidance in SKILL.md; move detailed reference material, schemas, and examples to references files.\r\n\r\n##### Assets (`assets/`)\r\n\r\nFiles not intended to be loaded into context, but rather used within the output Codex produces.\r\n\r\n- **When to include**: When the skill needs files that will be used in the final output\r\n- **Examples**: `assets/logo.png` for brand assets, `assets/slides.pptx` for PowerPoint templates, `assets/frontend-template/` for HTML/React boilerplate, `assets/font.ttf` for typography\r\n- **Use cases**: Templates, images, icons, boilerplate code, fonts, sample documents that get copied or modified\r\n- **Benefits**: Separates output resources from documentation, enables Codex to use files without loading them into context\r\n\r\n#### What to Not Include in a Skill\r\n\r\nA skill should only contain essential files that directly support its functionality. Do NOT create extraneous documentation or auxiliary files, including:\r\n\r\n- README.md\r\n- INSTALLATION_GUIDE.md\r\n- QUICK_REFERENCE.md\r\n- CHANGELOG.md\r\n- etc.\r\n\r\nThe skill should only contain the information needed for an AI agent to do the job at hand. It should not contain auxiliary context about the process that went into creating it, setup and testing procedures, user-facing documentation, etc. Creating additional documentation files just adds clutter and confusion.\r\n\r\n### Progressive Disclosure Design Principle\r\n\r\nSkills use a three-level loading system to manage context efficiently:\r\n\r\n1. **Metadata (name + description)** - Always in context (~100 words)\r\n2. **SKILL.md body** - When skill triggers (<5k words)\r\n3. **Bundled resources** - As needed by Codex (Unlimited because scripts can be executed without reading into context window)\r\n\r\n#### Progressive Disclosure Patterns\r\n\r\nKeep SKILL.md body to the essentials and under 500 lines to minimize context bloat. Split content into separate files when approaching this limit. When splitting out content into other files, it is very important to reference them from SKILL.md and describe clearly when to read them, to ensure the reader of the skill knows they exist and when to use them.\r\n\r\n**Key principle:** When a skill supports multiple variations, frameworks, or options, keep only the core workflow and selection guidance in SKILL.md. Move variant-specific details (patterns, examples, configuration) into separate reference files.\r\n\r\n**Pattern 1: High-level guide with references**\r\n\r\n```markdown\r\n# PDF Processing\r\n\r\n## Quick start\r\n\r\nExtract text with pdfplumber:\r\n[code example]\r\n\r\n## Advanced features\r\n\r\n- **Form filling**: See [FORMS.md](FORMS.md) for complete guide\r\n- **API reference**: See [REFERENCE.md](REFERENCE.md) for all methods\r\n- **Examples**: See [EXAMPLES.md](EXAMPLES.md) for common patterns\r\n```\r\n\r\nCodex loads FORMS.md, REFERENCE.md, or EXAMPLES.md only when needed.\r\n\r\n**Pattern 2: Domain-specific organization**\r\n\r\nFor Skills with multiple domains, organize content by domain to avoid loading irrelevant context:\r\n\r\n```\r\nbigquery-skill/\r\nΓö£ΓöÇΓöÇ SKILL.md (overview and navigation)\r\nΓööΓöÇΓöÇ reference/\r\n    Γö£ΓöÇΓöÇ finance.md (revenue, billing metrics)\r\n    Γö£ΓöÇΓöÇ sales.md (opportunities, pipeline)\r\n    Γö£ΓöÇΓöÇ product.md (API usage, features)\r\n    ΓööΓöÇΓöÇ marketing.md (campaigns, attribution)\r\n```\r\n\r\nWhen a user asks about sales metrics, Codex only reads sales.md.\r\n\r\nSimilarly, for skills supporting multiple frameworks or variants, organize by variant:\r\n\r\n```\r\ncloud-deploy/\r\nΓö£ΓöÇΓöÇ SKILL.md (workflow + provider selection)\r\nΓööΓöÇΓöÇ references/\r\n    Γö£ΓöÇΓöÇ aws.md (AWS deployment patterns)\r\n    Γö£ΓöÇΓöÇ gcp.md (GCP deployment patterns)\r\n    ΓööΓöÇΓöÇ azure.md (Azure deployment patterns)\r\n```\r\n\r\nWhen the user chooses AWS, Codex only reads aws.md.\r\n\r\n**Pattern 3: Conditional details**\r\n\r\nShow basic content, link to advanced content:\r\n\r\n```markdown\r\n# DOCX Processing\r\n\r\n## Creating documents\r\n\r\nUse docx-js for new documents. See [DOCX-JS.md](DOCX-JS.md).\r\n\r\n## Editing documents\r\n\r\nFor simple edits, modify the XML directly.\r\n\r\n**For tracked changes**: See [REDLINING.md](REDLINING.md)\r\n**For OOXML details**: See [OOXML.md](OOXML.md)\r\n```\r\n\r\nCodex reads REDLINING.md or OOXML.md only when the user needs those features.\r\n\r\n**Important guidelines:**\r\n\r\n- **Avoid deeply nested references** - Keep references one level deep from SKILL.md. All reference files should link directly from SKILL.md.\r\n- **Structure longer reference files** - For files longer than 100 lines, include a table of contents at the top so Codex can see the full scope when previewing.\r\n\r\n## Skill Creation Process\r\n\r\nSkill creation involves these steps:\r\n\r\n1. Understand the skill with concrete examples\r\n2. Plan reusable skill contents (scripts, references, assets)\r\n3. Initialize the skill (run init_skill.py)\r\n4. Edit the skill (implement resources and write SKILL.md)\r\n5. Validate the skill (run quick_validate.py)\r\n6. Iterate based on real usage and forward-test complex skills.\r\n\r\nFollow these steps in order, skipping only if there is a clear reason why they are not applicable.\r\n\r\n### Skill Naming\r\n\r\n- Use lowercase letters, digits, and hyphens only; normalize user-provided titles to hyphen-case (e.g., \"Plan Mode\" -> `plan-mode`).\r\n- When generating names, generate a name under 64 characters (letters, digits, hyphens).\r\n- Prefer short, verb-led phrases that describe the action.\r\n- Namespace by tool when it improves clarity or triggering (e.g., `gh-address-comments`, `linear-address-issue`).\r\n- Name the skill folder exactly after the skill name.\r\n\r\n### Step 1: Understanding the Skill with Concrete Examples\r\n\r\nSkip this step only when the skill's usage patterns are already clearly understood. It remains valuable even when working with an existing skill.\r\n\r\nTo create an effective skill, clearly understand concrete examples of how the skill will be used. This understanding can come from either direct user examples or generated examples that are validated with user feedback.\r\n\r\nFor example, when building an image-editor skill, relevant questions include:\r\n\r\n- \"What functionality should the image-editor skill support? Editing, rotating, anything else?\"\r\n- \"Can you give some examples of how this skill would be used?\"\r\n- \"I can imagine users asking for things like 'Remove the red-eye from this image' or 'Rotate this image'. Are there other ways you imagine this skill being used?\"\r\n- \"What would a user say that should trigger this skill?\"\r\n- \"Where should I create this skill? If you do not have a preference, I will place it in `$CODEX_HOME/skills` (or `~/.codex/skills` when `CODEX_HOME` is unset) so Codex can discover it automatically.\"\r\n\r\nTo avoid overwhelming users, avoid asking too many questions in a single message. Start with the most important questions and follow up as needed for better effectiveness.\r\n\r\nConclude this step when there is a clear sense of the functionality the skill should support.\r\n\r\n### Step 2: Planning the Reusable Skill Contents\r\n\r\nTo turn concrete examples into an effective skill, analyze each example by:\r\n\r\n1. Considering how to execute on the example from scratch\r\n2. Identifying what scripts, references, and assets would be helpful when executing these workflows repeatedly\r\n\r\nExample: When building a `pdf-editor` skill to handle queries like \"Help me rotate this PDF,\" the analysis shows:\r\n\r\n1. Rotating a PDF requires re-writing the same code each time\r\n2. A `scripts/rotate_pdf.py` script would be helpful to store in the skill\r\n\r\nExample: When designing a `frontend-webapp-builder` skill for queries like \"Build me a todo app\" or \"Build me a dashboard to track my steps,\" the analysis shows:\r\n\r\n1. Writing a frontend webapp requires the same boilerplate HTML/React each time\r\n2. An `assets/hello-world/` template containing the boilerplate HTML/React project files would be helpful to store in the skill\r\n\r\nExample: When building a `big-query` skill to handle queries like \"How many users have logged in today?\" the analysis shows:\r\n\r\n1. Querying BigQuery requires re-discovering the table schemas and relationships each time\r\n2. A `references/schema.md` file documenting the table schemas would be helpful to store in the skill\r\n\r\nTo establish the skill's contents, analyze each concrete example to create a list of the reusable resources to include: scripts, references, and assets.\r\n\r\n### Step 3: Initializing the Skill\r\n\r\nAt this point, it is time to actually create the skill.\r\n\r\nSkip this step only if the skill being developed already exists. In this case, continue to the next step.\r\n\r\nBefore running `init_skill.py`, ask where the user wants the skill created. If they do not specify a location, default to `$CODEX_HOME/skills`; when `CODEX_HOME` is unset, fall back to `~/.codex/skills` so the skill is auto-discovered.\r\n\r\nWhen creating a new skill from scratch, always run the `init_skill.py` script. The script conveniently generates a new template skill directory that automatically includes everything a skill requires, making the skill creation process much more efficient and reliable.\r\n\r\nUsage:\r\n\r\n```bash\r\nscripts/init_skill.py <skill-name> --path <output-directory> [--resources scripts,references,assets] [--examples]\r\n```\r\n\r\nExamples:\r\n\r\n```bash\r\nscripts/init_skill.py my-skill --path \"${CODEX_HOME:-$HOME/.codex}/skills\"\r\nscripts/init_skill.py my-skill --path \"${CODEX_HOME:-$HOME/.codex}/skills\" --resources scripts,references\r\nscripts/init_skill.py my-skill --path ~/work/skills --resources scripts --examples\r\n```\r\n\r\nThe script:\r\n\r\n- Creates the skill directory at the specified path\r\n- Generates a SKILL.md template with proper frontmatter and TODO placeholders\r\n- Creates `agents/openai.yaml` using agent-generated `display_name`, `short_description`, and `default_prompt` passed via `--interface key=value`\r\n- Optionally creates resource directories based on `--resources`\r\n- Optionally adds example files when `--examples` is set\r\n\r\nAfter initialization, customize the SKILL.md and add resources as needed. If you used `--examples`, replace or delete placeholder files.\r\n\r\nGenerate `display_name`, `short_description`, and `default_prompt` by reading the skill, then pass them as `--interface key=value` to `init_skill.py` or regenerate with:\r\n\r\n```bash\r\nscripts/generate_openai_yaml.py <path/to/skill-folder> --interface key=value\r\n```\r\n\r\nOnly include other optional interface fields when the user explicitly provides them. For full field descriptions and examples, see references/openai_yaml.md.\r\n\r\n### Step 4: Edit the Skill\r\n\r\nWhen editing the (newly-generated or existing) skill, remember that the skill is being created for another instance of Codex to use. Include information that would be beneficial and non-obvious to Codex. Consider what procedural knowledge, domain-specific details, or reusable assets would help another Codex instance execute these tasks more effectively.\r\n\r\nAfter substantial revisions, or if the skill is particularly tricky, you should use subagents to forward-test the skill on realistic tasks or artifacts. When doing so, pass the artifact under validation rather than your diagnosis of what is wrong, and keep the prompt generic enough that success depends on transferable reasoning rather than hidden ground truth.\r\n\r\n#### Start with Reusable Skill Contents\r\n\r\nTo begin implementation, start with the reusable resources identified above: `scripts/`, `references/`, and `assets/` files. Note that this step may require user input. For example, when implementing a `brand-guidelines` skill, the user may need to provide brand assets or templates to store in `assets/`, or documentation to store in `references/`.\r\n\r\nAdded scripts must be tested by actually running them to ensure there are no bugs and that the output matches what is expected. If there are many similar scripts, only a representative sample needs to be tested to ensure confidence that they all work while balancing time to completion.\r\n\r\nIf you used `--examples`, delete any placeholder files that are not needed for the skill. Only create resource directories that are actually required.\r\n\r\n#### Update SKILL.md\r\n\r\n**Writing Guidelines:** Always use imperative/infinitive form.\r\n\r\n##### Frontmatter\r\n\r\nWrite the YAML frontmatter with `name` and `description`:\r\n\r\n- `name`: The skill name\r\n- `description`: This is the primary triggering mechanism for your skill, and helps Codex understand when to use the skill.\r\n  - Include both what the Skill does and specific triggers/contexts for when to use it.\r\n  - Include all \"when to use\" information here - Not in the body. The body is only loaded after triggering, so \"When to Use This Skill\" sections in the body are not helpful to Codex.\r\n  - Example description for a `docx` skill: \"Comprehensive document creation, editing, and analysis with support for tracked changes, comments, formatting preservation, and text extraction. Use when Codex needs to work with professional documents (.docx files) for: (1) Creating new documents, (2) Modifying or editing content, (3) Working with tracked changes, (4) Adding comments, or any other document tasks\"\r\n\r\nDo not include any other fields in YAML frontmatter.\r\n\r\n##### Body\r\n\r\nWrite instructions for using the skill and its bundled resources.\r\n\r\n### Step 5: Validate the Skill\r\n\r\nOnce development of the skill is complete, validate the skill folder to catch basic issues early:\r\n\r\n```bash\r\nscripts/quick_validate.py <path/to/skill-folder>\r\n```\r\n\r\nThe validation script checks YAML frontmatter format, required fields, and naming rules. If validation fails, fix the reported issues and run the command again.\r\n\r\n### Step 6: Iterate\r\n\r\nAfter testing the skill, you may detect the skill is complex enough that it requires forward-testing; or users may request improvements.\r\n\r\nUser testing often this happens right after using the skill, with fresh context of how the skill performed.\r\n\r\n**Forward-testing and iteration workflow:**\r\n\r\n1. Use the skill on real tasks\r\n2. Notice struggles or inefficiencies\r\n3. Identify how SKILL.md or bundled resources should be updated\r\n4. Implement changes and test again\r\n5. Forward-test if it is reasonable and appropriate\r\n\r\n## Forward-testing\r\n\r\nTo forward-test, launch subagents as a way to stress test the skill with minimal context.\r\nSubagents should *not* know that they are being asked to test the skill.  They should be treated as\r\nan agent asked to perform a task by the user.  Prompts to subagents should look like:\r\n  `Use $skill-x at /path/to/skill-x to solve problem y`\r\nNot:\r\n  `Review the skill at /path/to/skill-x; pretend a user asks you to...`\r\n\r\nDecision rule for forward-testing:\r\n  - Err on the side of forward-testing\r\n  - Ask for approval if you think there's a risk that forward-testing would:\r\n    * take a long time,\r\n    * require additional approvals from the user, or\r\n    * modify live production systems\r\n\r\n  In these cases, show the user your proposed prompt and request (1) a yes/no decision, and\r\n  (2) any suggested modifictions.\r\n\r\nConsiderations when forward-testing:\r\n   - use fresh threads for independent passes\r\n   - pass the skill, and a request in a similar way the user would.\r\n   - pass raw artifacts, not your conclusions\r\n   - avoid showing expected answers or intended fixes\r\n   - rebuild context from source artifacts after each iteration\r\n   - review the subagent's output and reasoning and emitted artifacts\r\n   - avoid leaving artifacts the agent can find on disk between iterations;\r\n     clean up subagents' artifacts to avoid additional contamination.\r\n\r\nIf forward-testing only succeeds when subagents see leaked context, tighten the skill or the\r\nforward-testing setup before trusting the result.\r\n\r\n---REPO-STATE---\r\n?? .agents/\n?? .codex/\n?? .gitignore\n?? These are the only fields that Codex reads to determine when the skill gets used, thus it is very important to be clear and comprehensive in describing what the skill is, and when it should be used.\r\n- **Body** (Markdown): Instructions and guidance for using the skill. Only loaded AFTER the skill triggers (if at all).\r\n\r\n#### Agents metadata (recommended)\r\n\r\n- UI-facing metadata for skill lists and chips\r\n- Read references/openai_yaml.md before generating values and follow its descriptions and constraints\r\n- Create: human-facing `display_name`, `short_description`, and `default_prompt` by reading the skill\r\n- Generate deterministically by passing the values as `--interface key=value` to `scripts/generate_openai_yaml.py` or `scripts/init_skill.py`\r\n- On updates: validate `agents/openai.yaml` still matches SKILL.md; regenerate if stale\r\n- Only include other optional interface fields (icons, brand color) if explicitly provided\r\n- See references/openai_yaml.md for field definitions and examples\r\n\r\n#### Bundled Resources (optional)\r\n\r\n##### Scripts (`scripts/`)\r\n\r\nExecutable code (Python/Bash/etc.) for tasks that require deterministic reliability or are repeatedly rewritten.\r\n\r\n- **When to include**: When the same code is being rewritten repeatedly or deterministic reliability is needed\r\n- **Example**: `scripts/rotate_pdf.py` for PDF rotation tasks\r\n- **Benefits**: Token efficient, deterministic, may be executed without loading into context\r\n- **Note**: Scripts may still need to be read by Codex for patching or environment-specific adjustments\r\n\r\n##### References (`references/`)\r\n\r\nDocumentation and reference material intended to be loaded as needed into context to inform Codex's process and thinking.\r\n\r\n- **When to include**: For documentation that Codex should reference while working\r\n- **Examples**: `references/finance.md` for financial schemas, `references/mnda.md` for company NDA template, `references/policies.md` for company policies, `references/api_docs.md` for API specifications\r\n- **Use cases**: Database schemas, API documentation, domain knowledge, company policies, detailed workflow guides\r\n- **Benefits**: Keeps SKILL.md lean, loaded only when Codex determines it's needed\r\n- **Best practice**: If files are large (>10k words), include grep search patterns in SKILL.md\r\n- **Avoid duplication**: Information should live in either SKILL.md or references files, not both. Prefer references files for detailed information unless it's truly core to the skillΓÇöthis keeps SKILL.md lean while making information discoverable without hogging the context window. Keep only essential procedural instructions and workflow guidance in SKILL.md; move detailed reference material, schemas, and examples to references files.\r\n\r\n##### Assets (`assets/`)\r\n\r\nFiles not intended to be loaded into context, but rather used within the output Codex produces.\r\n\r\n- **When to include**: When the skill needs files that will be used in the final output\r\n- **Examples**: `assets/logo.png` for brand assets, `assets/slides.pptx` for PowerPoint templates, `assets/frontend-template/` for HTML/React boilerplate, `assets/font.ttf` for typography\r\n- **Use cases**: Templates, images, icons, boilerplate code, fonts, sample documents that get copied or modified\r\n- **Benefits**: Separates output resources from documentation, enables Codex to use files without loading them into context\r\n\r\n#### What to Not Include in a Skill\r\n\r\nA skill should only contain essential files that directly support its functionality. Do NOT create extraneous documentation or auxiliary files, including:\r\n\r\n- README.md\r\n- INSTALLATION_GUIDE.md\r\n- QUICK_REFERENCE.md\r\n- CHANGELOG.md\r\n- etc.\r\n\r\nThe skill should only contain the information needed for an AI agent to do the job at hand. It should not contain auxiliary context about the process that went into creating it, setup and testing procedures, user-facing documentation, etc. Creating additional documentation files just adds clutter and confusion.\r\n\r\n### Progressive Disclosure Design Principle\r\n\r\nSkills use a three-level loading system to manage context efficiently:\r\n\r\n1. **Metadata (name + description)** - Always in context (~100 words)\r\n2. **SKILL.md body** - When skill triggers (<5k words)\r\n3. **Bundled resources** - As needed by Codex (Unlimited because scripts can be executed without reading into context window)\r\n\r\n#### Progressive Disclosure Patterns\r\n\r\nKeep SKILL.md body to the essentials and under 500 lines to minimize context bloat. Split content into separate files when approaching this limit. When splitting out content into other files, it is very important to reference them from SKILL.md and describe clearly when to read them, to ensure the reader of the skill knows they exist and when to use them.\r\n\r\n**Key principle:** When a skill supports multiple variations, frameworks, or options, keep only the core workflow and selection guidance in SKILL.md. Move variant-specific details (patterns, examples, configuration) into separate reference files.\r\n\r\n**Pattern 1: High-level guide with references**\r\n\r\n```markdown\r\n# PDF Processing\r\n\r\n## Quick start\r\n\r\nExtract text with pdfplumber:\r\n[code example]\r\n\r\n## Advanced features\r\n\r\n- **Form filling**: See [FORMS.md](FORMS.md) for complete guide\r\n- **API reference**: See [REFERENCE.md](REFERENCE.md) for all methods\r\n- **Examples**: See [EXAMPLES.md](EXAMPLES.md) for common patterns\r\n```\r\n\r\nCodex loads FORMS.md, REFERENCE.md, or EXAMPLES.md only when needed.\r\n\r\n**Pattern 2: Domain-specific organization**\r\n\r\nFor Skills with multiple domains, organize content by domain to avoid loading irrelevant context:\r\n\r\n```\r\nbigquery-skill/\r\nΓö£ΓöÇΓöÇ SKILL.md (overview and navigation)\r\nΓööΓöÇΓöÇ reference/\r\n    Γö£ΓöÇΓöÇ finance.md (revenue, billing metrics)\r\n    Γö£ΓöÇΓöÇ sales.md (opportunities, pipeline)\r\n    Γö£ΓöÇΓöÇ product.md (API usage, features)\r\n    ΓööΓöÇΓöÇ marketing.md (campaigns, attribution)\r\n```\r\n\r\nWhen a user asks about sales metrics, Codex only reads sales.md.\r\n\r\nSimilarly, for skills supporting multiple frameworks or variants, organize by variant:\r\n\r\n```\r\ncloud-deploy/\r\nΓö£ΓöÇΓöÇ SKILL.md (workflow + provider selection)\r\nΓööΓöÇΓöÇ references/\r\n    Γö£ΓöÇΓöÇ aws.md (AWS deployment patterns)\r\n    Γö£ΓöÇΓöÇ gcp.md (GCP deployment patterns)\r\n    ΓööΓöÇΓöÇ azure.md (Azure deployment patterns)\r\n```\r\n\r\nWhen the user chooses AWS, Codex only reads aws.md.\r\n\r\n**Pattern 3: Conditional details**\r\n\r\nShow basic content, link to advanced content:\r\n\r\n```markdown\r\n# DOCX Processing\r\n\r\n## Creating documents\r\n\r\nUse docx-js for new documents. See [DOCX-JS.md](DOCX-JS.md).\r\n\r\n## Editing documents\r\n\r\nFor simple edits, modify the XML directly.\r\n\r\n**For tracked changes**: See [REDLINING.md](REDLINING.md)\r\n**For OOXML details**: See [OOXML.md](OOXML.md)\r\n```\r\n\r\nCodex reads REDLINING.md or OOXML.md only when the user needs those features.\r\n\r\n**Important guidelines:**\r\n\r\n- **Avoid deeply nested references** - Keep references one level deep from SKILL.md. All reference files should link directly from SKILL.md.\r\n- **Structure longer reference files** - For files longer than 100 lines, include a table of contents at the top so Codex can see the full scope when previewing.\r\n\r\n## Skill Creation Process\r\n\r\nSkill creation involves these steps:\r\n\r\n1. Understand the skill with concrete examples\r\n2. Plan reusable skill contents (scripts, references, assets)\r\n3. Initialize the skill (run init_skill.py)\r\n4. Edit the skill (implement resources and write SKILL.md)\r\n5. Validate the skill (run quick_validate.py)\r\n6. Iterate based on real usage and forward-test complex skills.\r\n\r\nFollow these steps in order, skipping only if there is a clear reason why they are not applicable.\r\n\r\n### Skill Naming\r\n\r\n- Use lowercase letters, digits, and hyphens only; normalize user-provided titles to hyphen-case (e.g., \"Plan Mode\" -> `plan-mode`).\r\n- When generating names, generate a name under 64 characters (letters, digits, hyphens).\r\n- Prefer short, verb-led phrases that describe the action.\r\n- Namespace by tool when it improves clarity or triggering (e.g., `gh-address-comments`, `linear-address-issue`).\r\n- Name the skill folder exactly after the skill name.\r\n\r\n### Step 1: Understanding the Skill with Concrete Examples\r\n\r\nSkip this step only when the skill's usage patterns are already clearly understood. It remains valuable even when working with an existing skill.\r\n\r\nTo create an effective skill, clearly understand concrete examples of how the skill will be used. This understanding can come from either direct user examples or generated examples that are validated with user feedback.\r\n\r\nFor example, when building an image-editor skill, relevant questions include:\r\n\r\n- \"What functionality should the image-editor skill support? Editing, rotating, anything else?\"\r\n- \"Can you give some examples of how this skill would be used?\"\r\n- \"I can imagine users asking for things like 'Remove the red-eye from this image' or 'Rotate this image'. Are there other ways you imagine this skill being used?\"\r\n- \"What would a user say that should trigger this skill?\"\r\n- \"Where should I create this skill? If you do not have a preference, I will place it in `$CODEX_HOME/skills` (or `~/.codex/skills` when `CODEX_HOME` is unset) so Codex can discover it automatically.\"\r\n\r\nTo avoid overwhelming users, avoid asking too many questions in a single message. Start with the most important questions and follow up as needed for better effectiveness.\r\n\r\nConclude this step when there is a clear sense of the functionality the skill should support.\r\n\r\n### Step 2: Planning the Reusable Skill Contents\r\n\r\nTo turn concrete examples into an effective skill, analyze each example by:\r\n\r\n1. Considering how to execute on the example from scratch\r\n2. Identifying what scripts, references, and assets would be helpful when executing these workflows repeatedly\r\n\r\nExample: When building a `pdf-editor` skill to handle queries like \"Help me rotate this PDF,\" the analysis shows:\r\n\r\n1. Rotating a PDF requires re-writing the same code each time\r\n2. A `scripts/rotate_pdf.py` script would be helpful to store in the skill\r\n\r\nExample: When designing a `frontend-webapp-builder` skill for queries like \"Build me a todo app\" or \"Build me a dashboard to track my steps,\" the analysis shows:\r\n\r\n1. Writing a frontend webapp requires the same boilerplate HTML/React each time\r\n2. An `assets/hello-world/` template containing the boilerplate HTML/React project files would be helpful to store in the skill\r\n\r\nExample: When building a `big-query` skill to handle queries like \"How many users have logged in today?\" the analysis shows:\r\n\r\n1. Querying BigQuery requires re-discovering the table schemas and relationships each time\r\n2. A `references/schema.md` file documenting the table schemas would be helpful to store in the skill\r\n\r\nTo establish the skill's contents, analyze each concrete example to create a list of the reusable resources to include: scripts, references, and assets.\r\n\r\n### Step 3: Initializing the Skill\r\n\r\nAt this point, it is time to actually create the skill.\r\n\r\nSkip this step only if the skill being developed already exists. In this case, continue to the next step.\r\n\r\nBefore running `init_skill.py`, ask where the user wants the skill created. If they do not specify a location, default to `$CODEX_HOME/skills`; when `CODEX_HOME` is unset, fall back to `~/.codex/skills` so the skill is auto-discovered.\r\n\r\nWhen creating a new skill from scratch, always run the `init_skill.py` script. The script conveniently generates a new template skill directory that automatically includes everything a skill requires, making the skill creation process much more efficient and reliable.\r\n\r\nUsage:\r\n\r\n```bash\r\nscripts/init_skill.py <skill-name> --path <output-directory> [--resources scripts,references,assets] [--examples]\r\n```\r\n\r\nExamples:\r\n\r\n```bash\r\nscripts/init_skill.py my-skill --path \"${CODEX_HOME:-$HOME/.codex}/skills\"\r\nscripts/init_skill.py my-skill --path \"${CODEX_HOME:-$HOME/.codex}/skills\" --resources scripts,references\r\nscripts/init_skill.py my-skill --path ~/work/skills --resources scripts --examples\r\n```\r\n\r\nThe script:\r\n\r\n- Creates the skill directory at the specified path\r\n- Generates a SKILL.md template with proper frontmatter and TODO placeholders\r\n- Creates `agents/openai.yaml` using agent-generated `display_name`, `short_description`, and `default_prompt` passed via `--interface key=value`\r\n- Optionally creates resource directories based on `--resources`\r\n- Optionally adds example files when `--examples` is set\r\n\r\nAfter initialization, customize the SKILL.md and add resources as needed. If you used `--examples`, replace or delete placeholder files.\r\n\r\nGenerate `display_name`, `short_description`, and `default_prompt` by reading the skill, then pass them as `--interface key=value` to `init_skill.py` or regenerate with:\r\n\r\n```bash\r\nscripts/generate_openai_yaml.py <path/to/skill-folder> --interface key=value\r\n```\r\n\r\nOnly include other optional interface fields when the user explicitly provides them. For full field descriptions and examples, see references/openai_yaml.md.\r\n\r\n### Step 4: Edit the Skill\r\n\r\nWhen editing the (newly-generated or existing) skill, remember that the skill is being created for another instance of Codex to use. Include information that would be beneficial and non-obvious to Codex. Consider what procedural knowledge, domain-specific details, or reusable assets would help another Codex instance execute these tasks more effectively.\r\n\r\nAfter substantial revisions, or if the skill is particularly tricky, you should use subagents to forward-test the skill on realistic tasks or artifacts. When doing so, pass the artifact under validation rather than your diagnosis of what is wrong, and keep the prompt generic enough that success depends on transferable reasoning rather than hidden ground truth.\r\n\r\n#### Start with Reusable Skill Contents\r\n\r\nTo begin implementation, start with the reusable resources identified above: `scripts/`, `references/`, and `assets/` files. Note that this step may require user input. For example, when implementing a `brand-guidelines` skill, the user may need to provide brand assets or templates to store in `assets/`, or documentation to store in `references/`.\r\n\r\nAdded scripts must be tested by actually running them to ensure there are no bugs and that the output matches what is expected. If there are many similar scripts, only a representative sample needs to be tested to ensure confidence that they all work while balancing time to completion.\r\n\r\nIf you used `--examples`, delete any placeholder files that are not needed for the skill. Only create resource directories that are actually required.\r\n\r\n#### Update SKILL.md\r\n\r\n**Writing Guidelines:** Always use imperative/infinitive form.\r\n\r\n##### Frontmatter\r\n\r\nWrite the YAML frontmatter with `name` and `description`:\r\n\r\n- `name`: The skill name\r\n- `description`: This is the primary triggering mechanism for your skill, and helps Codex understand when to use the skill.\r\n  - Include both what the Skill does and specific triggers/contexts for when to use it.\r\n  - Include all \"when to use\" information here - Not in the body. The body is only loaded after triggering, so \"When to Use This Skill\" sections in the body are not helpful to Codex.\r\n  - Example description for a `docx` skill: \"Comprehensive document creation, editing, and analysis with support for tracked changes, comments, formatting preservation, and text extraction. Use when Codex needs to work with professional documents (.docx files) for: (1) Creating new documents, (2) Modifying or editing content, (3) Working with tracked changes, (4) Adding comments, or any other document tasks\"\r\n\r\nDo not include any other fields in YAML frontmatter.\r\n\r\n##### Body\r\n\r\nWrite instructions for using the skill and its bundled resources.\r\n\r\n### Step 5: Validate the Skill\r\n\r\nOnce development of the skill is complete, validate the skill folder to catch basic issues early:\r\n\r\n```bash\r\nscripts/quick_validate.py <path/to/skill-folder>\r\n```\r\n\r\nThe validation script checks YAML frontmatter format, required fields, and naming rules. If validation fails, fix the reported issues and run the command again.\r\n\r\n### Step 6: Iterate\r\n\r\nAfter testing the skill, you may detect the skill is complex enough that it requires forward-testing; or users may request improvements.\r\n\r\nUser testing often this happens right after using the skill, with fresh context of how the skill performed.\r\n\r\n**Forward-testing and iteration workflow:**\r\n\r\n1. Use the skill on real tasks\r\n2. Notice struggles or inefficiencies\r\n3. Identify how SKILL.md or bundled resources should be updated\r\n4. Implement changes and test again\r\n5. Forward-test if it is reasonable and appropriate\r\n\r\n## Forward-testing\r\n\r\nTo forward-test, launch subagents as a way to stress test the skill with minimal context.\r\nSubagents should *not* know that they are being asked to test the skill.  They should be treated as\r\nan agent asked to perform a task by the user.  Prompts to subagents should look like:\r\n  `Use $skill-x at /path/to/skill-x to solve problem y`\r\nNot:\r\n  `Review the skill at /path/to/skill-x; pretend a user asks you to...`\r\n\r\nDecision rule for forward-testing:\r\n  - Err on the side of forward-testing\r\n  - Ask for approval if you think there's a risk that forward-testing would:\r\n    * take a long time,\r\n    * require additional approvals from the user, or\r\n    * modify live production systems\r\n\r\n  In these cases, show the user your proposed prompt and request (1) a yes/no decision, and\r\n  (2) any suggested modifictions.\r\n\r\nConsiderations when forward-testing:\r\n   - use fresh threads for independent passes\r\n   - pass the skill, and a request in a similar way the user would.\r\n   - pass raw artifacts, not your conclusions\r\n   - avoid showing expected answers or intended fixes\r\n   - rebuild context from source artifacts after each iteration\r\n   - review the subagent's output and reasoning and emitted artifacts\r\n   - avoid leaving artifacts the agent can find on disk between iterations;\r\n     clean up subagents' artifacts to avoid additional contamination.\r\n\r\nIf forward-testing only succeeds when subagents see leaked context, tighten the skill or the\r\nforward-testing setup before trusting the result.\r\n\r\n---STATE---\r\n?? .agents/\n?? .codex/\n?? .gitignore\n?? Execute every call, then append one tool message per call, each with its own tool_call_id, before the next request. The multi-turn example above already loops over tool_calls to do this. To limit the model to one call per turn, set parallel_tool_calls: false (default true). This flag takes effect only when you provide function tools; with no function tools it is accepted but has no effect, matching OpenAI. It applies to both Chat Completions and the [**Responses API**](https://dev.meta.ai/docs/features/responses?project_id=993433083592653&team_id=1731068077918279).\r\nΓÇó**max\\_tool\\_calls limits built-in tools only**: max_tool_calls caps the model's **built-in** tool calls (such as web_search), counted across all built-in tools; the model ignores calls beyond the limit. It has a minimum of 1 and no enforced maximum. It does not limit client-side function-tool calls. To bound function-tool calls, set parallel_tool_calls: false or cap turns in your own loop.\r\nΓÇó**tool\\_choice must be \"auto\"**: Only \"auto\" (the default) is supported on both Chat Completions and the [**Responses API**](https://dev.meta.ai/docs/features/responses?project_id=993433083592653&team_id=1731068077918279); \"none\", \"required\", and named function choices return HTTP 400 (\"only \"auto\" is supported for tool_choice\"). With \"auto\", the model decides whether to call a tool, so your app should handle both a tool call and a plain text response.\r\nΓÇó**Tool-call arguments stream**: With stream: true, the model streams arguments incrementally. On Chat Completions, accumulate tool_calls deltas across chunks by index; on the [**Responses API**](https://dev.meta.ai/docs/features/responses?project_id=993433083592653&team_id=1731068077918279), consume response.function_call_arguments.delta events and finalize on response.function_call_arguments.done.\r\nΓÇó**Always include the full assistant message**: When returning tool results, include the complete assistant message with its tool_calls array before the tool message. Omitting it returns HTTP 400.\r\nΓÇó**Match tool\\_call\\_id / call\\_id to the originating call**: On Chat Completions, each tool message must carry the tool_call_id of the call it answers. On the Responses API, when you construct input manually without previous_response_id, every function_call_output.call_id must match a function_call.call_id in the same request; a mismatch returns HTTP 400. With previous_response_id, the server resolves these from stored history.\r\nΓÇó**Keep call\\_id within 1ΓÇô64 characters**: Every call_id on both function_call and function_call_output items must be 1 to 64 characters. An empty or overlength call_id returns HTTP 400.\r\nΓÇó**Tool name validation applies only to the most recent assistant turn**: When you provide a tools array, the server validates that tool_calls[].function.name matches a defined tool name. Historical assistant messages with tool calls that reference tools no longer in the current tools array do not cause validation errors, as long as those calls already have corresponding tool results in history.\r\nΓÇó**Use tools, not deprecated fields**: functions and function_call are deprecated. Use tools and tool_choice.\r\nΓÇó**Use structured output for complex arguments**: If you need strict control over tool argument formats, combine tool calling with [**structured output**](https://dev.meta.ai/docs/features/structured-output?project_id=993433083592653&team_id=1731068077918279) via response_format.\r\nΓÇó**Defer large tool sets**: When you have many tools, front-loading every definition wastes tokens. A text match is not proof of\nactive ownership.\n\n## Authority risk\n\nDo not create, promote, replace, or redirect without explicit approval:\nstate roots; runtime entrypoints; execution authorities; registries;\nlaunchers; resolvers; runners; output writers; mutation authorities;\ndeployment authorities; parallel implementation paths.\n\nWhen authority cannot be determined, state `I don't know`, then explain\nwhat was checked, what remains unknown, what evidence is missing, what is\nblocked, and the next evidence step.\n\n## Mutation\n\nBefore changing files:\n\n1. Verify the active implementation.\n2. Confirm approved scope.\n3. Confirm intended touched paths.\n4. Separate unrelated dirty files.\n5. Establish rollback.\n6. Run required available pre-change validators.\n7. Confirm no unresolved authority conflict exists.\n\nDuring mutation: remain inside approved paths; preserve unrelated work;\navoid duplicate ownership; avoid speculative refactoring; avoid widening\nscope without approval.\n\nAfter mutation:\n\n1. Inspect the exact diff.\n2. Confirm only intended files changed.\n3. Run focused validators.\n4. Run broader regression checks when the change touches a shared/critical\n   path ΓÇö entrypoints, shared modules, public interfaces ΓÇö or when a nested\n   file specifies it; otherwise focused validation is sufficient, but state\n   which case applied.\n5. Report failures and unverified areas.\n6. Stop if the diff exceeds approved scope.\n\nDo not stage, commit, push, publish, deploy, or release unless explicitly\nrequested. \"Explicitly requested\" means the current-conversation user\ninstruction names the specific action and target (e.g. \"push this to\norigin/main\") ΓÇö a general task description or prior-session approval does\nnot imply it.\n\n## Validation\n\nValidation must cover the active production path when runtime behavior is\nbeing changed. Test-only helpers do not prove production integration. A\npassing unit test does not independently prove entrypoint reachability,\npackage inclusion, deployment behavior, external-service compatibility, or\nruntime ownership.\n\nFor every validation claim, include: exact command; relevant output; exit\ncode; touched paths; interpretation. Do not claim success when required\nvalidation is incomplete.\n\n## Evaluation and proof review\n\nJudge only the artifacts provided or inspected during the current task.\nEvidence may include expectations, transcripts, output files, proof\npackets, validation reports, assertion results, run IDs, task artifacts.\n\nIf no relevant artifact is available, state that there is no evidence to\nevaluate. Do not infer hidden runs, hidden data, hidden implementation, or\nhidden output quality.\n\nFor each verdict, state what was required, what was checked, what evidence\nsupports the result, what was missing or contradicted. Classify each\nexpectation using the Diagnostic-evidence vocabulary ΓÇö `valid` / `not_valid`\nΓÇö and use `uncertainty` when evidence is genuinely mixed or incomplete. Do\nnot use \"pass\"/\"fail\" as bare words; they are not part of the closed\nvocabulary.\n\nFor comparisons, remain blind to producer identity. Judge correctness,\ncompleteness, evidence use, constraint compliance, task completion, output\nquality.\n\n## Reporting\n\nAfter mutation, report:\n\n```text\nChanged:\nCommands_Run:\nResult:\nEvidence:\nStop_Condition:\n```\n\n`Changed` identifies touched paths and confirms unrelated changes were\npreserved.\n\n`Commands_Run` includes exact commands and exit codes.\n\n`Result` uses the Execution-state vocabulary only (`completed` / `failed` /\n`blocked` / `not_run` / `skipped`) ΓÇö never `Passed` or any term outside that\nset. If a Diagnostic-evidence or Proposal/apply-state claim is also\nrelevant, state it as its own labeled line rather than folding it into\n`Result`.\n\n`Evidence` connects material claims to inspected files or command output.\n\n`Stop_Condition` ΓÇö if `Result` is `blocked`, it must state: what produced\nthe block; which action is blocked; why; the evidence; the impact if the\nblock remains; the risk if unblocked incorrectly; and the recommended next\naction. Otherwise, it states why work stopped (task complete, approval\nrequired, evidence insufficient, etc.).\n\n## Learning capture\n\nPropose a reusable lesson only when the task exposes a failure mode that\ncould prevent future repository drift, authority confusion, scope\nexpansion, duplicate ownership, or evidence misuse. The agent may propose\nthe lesson. The user must approve it before it becomes repository\ninstruction ΓÇö and approved lessons that are genuinely global go here; ones\nthat are repo-specific go in that repo's nested file.\n\n## Stop conditions\n\nStop when: the approved task is complete; user approval is required;\nevidence is insufficient; authority instructions conflict; validation\nfails; dirty-state risk is unresolved; scope would expand; destructive\nmutation is required; rollback is unavailable; the next action would\ncreate or promote a new authority path.\n\nState the exact stop condition and the supporting evidence.\n\n## Plan mode\n\nPlan mode governs tasks where the user asks for a plan before execution, or\nwhere scope/risk (authority-boundary changes, multi-file mutation,\nrelease-adjacent work) warrants a written plan before touching anything. For\nsmaller, single-path tasks, the General task review gate above is\nsufficient on its own. Plan mode requires two distinct passes. Do not\npresent the initial draft as the final plan before completing the gap\nreview and success definition.\n\n### First pass: Draft plan\n\nCreate a task-specific plan based on the user's request, approved scope,\nactive implementation, applicable authority instructions, available\nevidence, required validation, and known constraints/risks.\n\nThe draft plan must identify: objective; interpretation; target; scope;\nexcluded work; ordered actions; expected touched paths when mutation is\nexpected later; dependencies; authority risks; validation requirements;\nrollback approach; stop conditions.\n\nDo not mutate files during plan mode unless the user explicitly authorizes\nexecution.\n\n### Primary-agent plan completion check\n\nAfter the draft plan exists, the primary agent checks it against the\napproved scope, repository evidence, authority boundaries, dependencies, and\nproposed validation commands. It identifies material gaps and unsupported\nassumptions; missing dependencies, authority risks, or scope expansion;\nconcrete validation and failure cases; measurable success criteria; stop\nconditions; and decisions requiring user approval. Do not request or invoke\nany review agent or parent review. If the check finds material ambiguity,\nauthority risk, scope expansion, or a destructive action requiring approval,\nask the user before implementation.\n\n### Second pass: Plan gap check\n\nRun a separate primary-agent check directly against the draft plan, determining: whether\nevery user requirement is represented; whether any step exceeds approved\nscope; whether the plan assumes unverified repository behavior; whether\nactive ownership and authority are known; whether dependencies and\nprerequisites are identified; whether steps are ordered correctly; whether\nrequired evidence is available; whether validation can prove the intended\nresult; whether rollback is possible; whether the plan creates duplicate or\nparallel authority; whether any step is vague, non-executable,\ncontradictory, or unnecessary; whether a required decision still needs user\napproval.\n\nFor every identified gap, state: the affected plan step; what is missing\nor contradictory; why the gap matters; the required correction; whether the\ngap blocks execution.\n\nRevise the draft plan to resolve all material gaps that can be resolved\nwithout changing user intent or approved scope. Do not silently change the\nrequested architecture or substitute a different design while correcting\nthe plan.\n\n### Success definition\n\nAfter the gap review, explicitly state what successful completion looks\nlike: specific to the task; measurable or directly inspectable; consistent\nwith the user's request and repository authority; sufficient to\ndistinguish completion from partial completion; linked to concrete\nvalidation commands or evidence when execution is involved.\n\nDo not use vague success statements (\"the implementation works\", \"the task\nis complete\", \"all issues are fixed\"). Use verifiable statements ΓÇö e.g.\nthe canonical entrypoint reaches the changed implementation; only the\napproved target files differ from the pre-change state; the focused\nvalidator and required regression suite exit `completed`; the resulting\noutput matches the required schema and preserves all required identifiers;\nno unresolved authority conflict or material validation gap remains.\n\n### Plan acceptance rule\n\nA plan is ready for execution only when: the draft plan exists, and the\nplan gap review is complete, and all material requirements are\nrepresented, and all executable steps are sufficiently specific, and\nauthority risks are resolved or explicitly blocked, and validation\nrequirements are defined, and successful completion is explicitly\ndescribed.\n\nIf a material gap remains, mark the plan `blocked` and state the\nunresolved gap, why it blocks execution, the evidence or approval\nrequired, and the next permitted action.\n\n--- project-doc ---\n\n# Agents.md ΓÇö Theoneshot (repo instance)\r\n\r\nSave as `D:\\Dev\\Theoneshot\\Agents.md`. Judge correctness,\ncompleteness, evidence use, constraint compliance, task completion, output\nquality.\n\n## Reporting\n\nAfter mutation, report:\n\n```text\nChanged:\nCommands_Run:\nResult:\nEvidence:\nStop_Condition:\n```\n\n`Changed` identifies touched paths and confirms unrelated changes were\npreserved.\n\n`Commands_Run` includes exact commands and exit codes.\n\n`Result` uses the Execution-state vocabulary only (`completed` / `failed` /\n`blocked` / `not_run` / `skipped`) ΓÇö never `Passed` or any term outside that\nset. If a Diagnostic-evidence or Proposal/apply-state claim is also\nrelevant, state it as its own labeled line rather than folding it into\n`Result`.\n\n`Evidence` connects material claims to inspected files or command output.\n\n`Stop_Condition` ΓÇö if `Result` is `blocked`, it must state: what produced\nthe block; which action is blocked; why; the evidence; the impact if the\nblock remains; the risk if unblocked incorrectly; and the recommended next\naction. Otherwise, it states why work stopped (task complete, approval\nrequired, evidence insufficient, etc.).\n\n## Learning capture\n\nPropose a reusable lesson only when the task exposes a failure mode that\ncould prevent future repository drift, authority confusion, scope\nexpansion, duplicate ownership, or evidence misuse. The agent may propose\nthe lesson. The user must approve it before it becomes repository\ninstruction ΓÇö and approved lessons that are genuinely global go here; ones\nthat are repo-specific go in that repo's nested file.\n\n## Stop conditions\n\nStop when: the approved task is complete; user approval is required;\nevidence is insufficient; authority instructions conflict; validation\nfails; dirty-state risk is unresolved; scope would expand; destructive\nmutation is required; rollback is unavailable; the next action would\ncreate or promote a new authority path.\n\nState the exact stop condition and the supporting evidence.\n\n## Plan mode\n\nPlan mode governs tasks where the user asks for a plan before execution, or\nwhere scope/risk (authority-boundary changes, multi-file mutation,\nrelease-adjacent work) warrants a written plan before touching anything. For\nsmaller, single-path tasks, the General task review gate above is\nsufficient on its own. Plan mode requires two distinct passes. Do not\npresent the initial draft as the final plan before completing the gap\nreview and success definition.\n\n### First pass: Draft plan\n\nCreate a task-specific plan based on the user's request, approved scope,\nactive implementation, applicable authority instructions, available\nevidence, required validation, and known constraints/risks.\n\nThe draft plan must identify: objective; interpretation; target; scope;\nexcluded work; ordered actions; expected touched paths when mutation is\nexpected later; dependencies; authority risks; validation requirements;\nrollback approach; stop conditions.\n\nDo not mutate files during plan mode unless the user explicitly authorizes\nexecution.\n\n### Primary-agent plan completion check\n\nAfter the draft plan exists, the primary agent checks it against the\napproved scope, repository evidence, authority boundaries, dependencies, and\nproposed validation commands. Do not request or invoke\nany review agent or parent review. Execute every call, then append one tool message per call, each with its own tool_call_id, before the next request. The multi-turn example above already loops over tool_calls to do this. To limit the model to one call per turn, set parallel_tool_calls: false (default true). This flag takes effect only when you provide function tools; with no function tools it is accepted but has no effect, matching OpenAI. It applies to both Chat Completions and the [**Responses API**](https://dev.meta.ai/docs/features/responses?project_id=993433083592653&team_id=1731068077918279).\r\nΓÇó**max\\_tool\\_calls limits built-in tools only**: max_tool_calls caps the model's **built-in** tool calls (such as web_search), counted across all built-in tools; the model ignores calls beyond the limit. It has a minimum of 1 and no enforced maximum. It does not limit client-side function-tool calls. To bound function-tool calls, set parallel_tool_calls: false or cap turns in your own loop.\r\nΓÇó**tool\\_choice must be \"auto\"**: Only \"auto\" (the default) is supported on both Chat Completions and the [**Responses API**](https://dev.meta.ai/docs/features/responses?project_id=993433083592653&team_id=1731068077918279); \"none\", \"required\", and named function choices return HTTP 400 (\"only \"auto\" is supported for tool_choice\"). With \"auto\", the model decides whether to call a tool, so your app should handle both a tool call and a plain text response.\r\nΓÇó**Tool-call arguments stream**: With stream: true, the model streams arguments incrementally. On Chat Completions, accumulate tool_calls deltas across chunks by index; on the [**Responses API**](https://dev.meta.ai/docs/features/responses?project_id=993433083592653&team_id=1731068077918279), consume response.function_call_arguments.delta events and finalize on response.function_call_arguments.done.\r\nΓÇó**Always include the full assistant message**: When returning tool results, include the complete assistant message with its tool_calls array before the tool message. Omitting it returns HTTP 400.\r\nΓÇó**Match tool\\_call\\_id / call\\_id to the originating call**: On Chat Completions, each tool message must carry the tool_call_id of the call it answers. On the Responses API, when you construct input manually without previous_response_id, every function_call_output.call_id must match a function_call.call_id in the same request; a mismatch returns HTTP 400. With previous_response_id, the server resolves these from stored history.\r\nΓÇó**Keep call\\_id within 1ΓÇô64 characters**: Every call_id on both function_call and function_call_output items must be 1 to 64 characters. An empty or overlength call_id returns HTTP 400.\r\nΓÇó**Tool name validation applies only to the most recent assistant turn**: When you provide a tools array, the server validates that tool_calls[].function.name matches a defined tool name. Historical assistant messages with tool calls that reference tools no longer in the current tools array do not cause validation errors, as long as those calls already have corresponding tool results in history.\r\nΓÇó**Use tools, not deprecated fields**: functions and function_call are deprecated. Do not fix unrelated findings while\ninspecting. A narrow request gets a narrow answer ΓÇö do not expand scope,\nadd adjacent workflow, or continue past the requested deliverable.\n\n## Status vocabulary\n\nAll status, verdict, and label language must come from one of the three\nclosed sets below. All-caps general-status words (`PASS`, `BLOCK`, `FAIL`,\n`COMPLETE`, `WARN`, and similar) are **blacklisted** for general use. The\nonly exception: quoting an external tool/command identifier verbatim ΓÇö in\nthat case, wrap it as `contract_label` and pair it with scope, evidence,\nimpact, and next action, so the raw external label is never presented as if\nit were this file's own verdict.\n\n* **Diagnostic evidence:** `valid` / `not_valid` / `uncertainty`\n* **Execution state:** `completed` / `failed` / `blocked` / `not_run` / `skipped`\n* **Proposal / apply state:** `proposal_only` / `review_required` /\n  `approved_for_apply` / `not_approved` / `already_applied` / `idempotent` /\n  `missing_parent` / `protected_surface`\n\nWhich set applies to which report field is fixed in Reporting, below ΓÇö do\nnot mix sets within a single field.\n\nWhen evidence for execution is missing, the state is `not_run` and the\nreport must say so explicitly as `Unverified_Execution_Claim` ΓÇö never\ninferred, never left blank.\n\n## Evidence\n\nEvidence must come before claims or mutation.\n\nFor repository-state, runtime, validation, mutation, or release claims,\nreport: repository path; branch; `HEAD`; dirty status; command; relevant\noutput excerpt; exit code; interpretation.\n\nBefore including captured command output in any report, redact credentials,\ntokens, keys, and secrets. Note that redaction occurred; never reproduce the\nredacted value, even partially.\n\nFor scans, state the included and excluded paths or globs.\n\nDo not treat memory, previous conversations, old reports, prior plans, or\nearlier command output as current evidence.\n\nWhen execution proof is missing, use `Unverified_Execution_Claim` (see\nStatus vocabulary). Do not invent command output, exit codes, pass counts,\nruntime behavior, file contents, deployment results, publication status, or\nsuccess labels.\n\n## Repository state\n\nBefore mutation, identify: user request; interpretation; requirement\nconflicts; target paths; excluded paths; branch; `HEAD`; dirty status;\nexpected touched paths; unrelated dirty paths; rollback path; authority\nrisk; required validators.\n\nA dirty repository blocks mutation unless the task is specifically about\nresolving the dirty state, or the user approves after dirty paths are\ndisclosed and separated from intended changes.\n\nNever reset, clean, stash, overwrite, stage, commit, or discard unrelated\nwork. Recheck repository state immediately before writing.\n\n## Active implementation\n\nDo not treat a component as active merely because its file or name exists.\nBefore claiming runtime ownership or activation, determine where it is\ndefined, what imports it, what calls it, whether the canonical entrypoint\nreaches it, whether it is packaged, whether it is tested, whether it is\ndeployed.\n\nClassify relevant components as: active / generated / historical / advisory\n/ compatibility / experimental / test-only / residue.\n\nDo not perform blind global replacement. A text match is not proof of\nactive ownership.\n\n## Authority risk\n\nDo not create, promote, replace, or redirect without explicit approval:\nstate roots; runtime entrypoints; execution authorities; registries;\nlaunchers; resolvers; runners; output writers; mutation authorities;\ndeployment authorities; parallel implementation paths.\n\nWhen authority cannot be determined, state `I don't know`, then explain\nwhat was checked, what remains unknown, what evidence is missing, what is\nblocked, and the next evidence step.\n\n## Mutation\n\nBefore changing files:\n\n1. Verify the active implementation.\n2. Confirm approved scope.\n3. Confirm intended touched paths.\n4. Separate unrelated dirty files.\n5. Establish rollback.\n6. Run required available pre-change validators.\n7. Confirm no unresolved authority conflict exists.\n\nDuring mutation: remain inside approved paths; preserve unrelated work;\navoid duplicate ownership; avoid speculative refactoring; avoid widening\nscope without approval.\n\nAfter mutation:\n\n1. Inspect the exact diff.\n2. Confirm only intended files changed.\n3. Run focused validators.\n4. Run broader regression checks when the change touches a shared/critical\n   path ΓÇö entrypoints, shared modules, public interfaces ΓÇö or when a nested\n   file specifies it; otherwise focused validation is sufficient, but state\n   which case applied.\n5. Report failures and unverified areas.\n6. Stop if the diff exceeds approved scope.\n\nDo not stage, commit, push, publish, deploy, or release unless explicitly\nrequested. \"Explicitly requested\" means the current-conversation user\ninstruction names the specific action and target (e.g. \"push this to\norigin/main\") ΓÇö a general task description or prior-session approval does\nnot imply it.\n\n## Validation\n\nValidation must cover the active production path when runtime behavior is\nbeing changed. Test-only helpers do not prove production integration. A\npassing unit test does not independently prove entrypoint reachability,\npackage inclusion, deployment behavior, external-service compatibility, or\nruntime ownership.\n\nFor every validation claim, include: exact command; relevant output; exit\ncode; touched paths; interpretation. Do not claim success when required\nvalidation is incomplete.\n\n## Evaluation and proof review\n\nJudge only the artifacts provided or inspected during the current task.\nEvidence may include expectations, transcripts, output files, proof\npackets, validation reports, assertion results, run IDs, task artifacts.\n\nIf no relevant artifact is available, state that there is no evidence to\nevaluate. Do not infer hidden runs, hidden data, hidden implementation, or\nhidden output quality.\n\nFor each verdict, state what was required, what was checked, what evidence\nsupports the result, what was missing or contradicted. Classify each\nexpectation using the Diagnostic-evidence vocabulary ΓÇö `valid` / `not_valid`\nΓÇö and use `uncertainty` when evidence is genuinely mixed or incomplete. Do\nnot use \"pass\"/\"fail\" as bare words; they are not part of the closed\nvocabulary.\n\nFor comparisons, remain blind to producer identity. Judge correctness,\ncompleteness, evidence use, constraint compliance, task completion, output\nquality.\n\n## Reporting\n\nAfter mutation, report:\n\n```text\nChanged:\nCommands_Run:\nResult:\nEvidence:\nStop_Condition:\n```\n\n`Changed` identifies touched paths and confirms unrelated changes were\npreserved.\n\n`Commands_Run` includes exact commands and exit codes.\n\n`Result` uses the Execution-state vocabulary only (`completed` / `failed` /\n`blocked` / `not_run` / `skipped`) ΓÇö never `Passed` or any term outside that\nset. If a Diagnostic-evidence or Proposal/apply-state claim is also\nrelevant, state it as its own labeled line rather than folding it into\n`Result`.\n\n`Evidence` connects material claims to inspected files or command output.\n\n`Stop_Condition` ΓÇö if `Result` is `blocked`, it must state: what produced\nthe block; which action is blocked; why; the evidence; the impact if the\nblock remains; the risk if unblocked incorrectly; and the recommended next\naction. Otherwise, it states why work stopped (task complete, approval\nrequired, evidence insufficient, etc.).\n\n## Learning capture\n\nPropose a reusable lesson only when the task exposes a failure mode that\ncould prevent future repository drift, authority confusion, scope\nexpansion, duplicate ownership, or evidence misuse. The agent may propose\nthe lesson. The user must approve it before it becomes repository\ninstruction ΓÇö and approved lessons that are genuinely global go here; ones\nthat are repo-specific go in that repo's nested file.\n\n## Stop conditions\n\nStop when: the approved task is complete; user approval is required;\nevidence is insufficient; authority instructions conflict; validation\nfails; dirty-state risk is unresolved; scope would expand; destructive\nmutation is required; rollback is unavailable; the next action would\ncreate or promote a new authority path.\n\nState the exact stop condition and the supporting evidence.\n\n## Plan mode\n\nPlan mode governs tasks where the user asks for a plan before execution, or\nwhere scope/risk (authority-boundary changes, multi-file mutation,\nrelease-adjacent work) warrants a written plan before touching anything. For\nsmaller, single-path tasks, the General task review gate above is\nsufficient on its own. Plan mode requires two distinct passes. Do not\npresent the initial draft as the final plan before completing the gap\nreview and success definition.\n\n### First pass: Draft plan\n\nCreate a task-specific plan based on the user's request, approved scope,\nactive implementation, applicable authority instructions, available\nevidence, required validation, and known constraints/risks.\n\nThe draft plan must identify: objective; interpretation; target; scope;\nexcluded work; ordered actions; expected touched paths when mutation is\nexpected later; dependencies; authority risks; validation requirements;\nrollback approach; stop conditions.\n\nDo not mutate files during plan mode unless the user explicitly authorizes\nexecution.\n\n### Primary-agent plan completion check\n\nAfter the draft plan exists, the primary agent checks it against the\napproved scope, repository evidence, authority boundaries, dependencies, and\nproposed validation commands. It identifies material gaps and unsupported\nassumptions; missing dependencies, authority risks, or scope expansion;\nconcrete validation and failure cases; measurable success criteria; stop\nconditions; and decisions requiring user approval. Do not request or invoke\nany review agent or parent review. If the check finds material ambiguity,\nauthority risk, scope expansion, or a destructive action requiring approval,\nask the user before implementation.\n\n### Second pass: Plan gap check\n\nRun a separate primary-agent check directly against the draft plan, determining: whether\nevery user requirement is represented; whether any step exceeds approved\nscope; whether the plan assumes unverified repository behavior; whether\nactive ownership and authority are known; whether dependencies and\nprerequisites are identified; whether steps are ordered correctly; whether\nrequired evidence is available; whether validation can prove the intended\nresult; whether rollback is possible; whether the plan creates duplicate or\nparallel authority; whether any step is vague, non-executable,\ncontradictory, or unnecessary; whether a required decision still needs user\napproval.\n\nFor every identified gap, state: the affected plan step; what is missing\nor contradictory; why the gap matters; the required correction; whether the\ngap blocks execution.\n\nRevise the draft plan to resolve all material gaps that can be resolved\nwithout changing user intent or approved scope. Do not silently change the\nrequested architecture or substitute a different design while correcting\nthe plan.\n\n### Success definition\n\nAfter the gap review, explicitly state what successful completion looks\nlike: specific to the task; measurable or directly inspectable; consistent\nwith the user's request and repository authority; sufficient to\ndistinguish completion from partial completion; linked to concrete\nvalidation commands or evidence when execution is involved.\n\nDo not use vague success statements (\"the implementation works\", \"the task\nis complete\", \"all issues are fixed\"). Use verifiable statements ΓÇö e.g.\nthe canonical entrypoint reaches the changed implementation; only the\napproved target files differ from the pre-change state; the focused\nvalidator and required regression suite exit `completed`; the resulting\noutput matches the required schema and preserves all required identifiers;\nno unresolved authority conflict or material validation gap remains.\n\n### Plan acceptance rule\n\nA plan is ready for execution only when: the draft plan exists, and the\nplan gap review is complete, and all material requirements are\nrepresented, and all executable steps are sufficiently specific, and\nauthority risks are resolved or explicitly blocked, and validation\nrequirements are defined, and successful completion is explicitly\ndescribed.\n\nIf a material gap remains, mark the plan `blocked` and state the\nunresolved gap, why it blocks execution, the evidence or approval\nrequired, and the next permitted action.\n\n--- project-doc ---\n\n# Agents.md ΓÇö Theoneshot (repo instance)\r\n\r\nSave as `D:\\Dev\\Theoneshot\\Agents.md`. Run broader regression checks when the change touches a shared/critical\n   path ΓÇö entrypoints, shared modules, public interfaces ΓÇö or when a nested\n   file specifies it; otherwise focused validation is sufficient, but state\n   which case applied.\n5. Report failures and unverified areas.\n6. Stop if the diff exceeds approved scope.\n\nDo not stage, commit, push, publish, deploy, or release unless explicitly\nrequested. \"Explicitly requested\" means the current-conversation user\ninstruction names the specific action and target (e.g. \"push this to\norigin/main\") ΓÇö a general task description or prior-session approval does\nnot imply it.\n\n## Validation\n\nValidation must cover the active production path when runtime behavior is\nbeing changed. Test-only helpers do not prove production integration. A\npassing unit test does not independently prove entrypoint reachability,\npackage inclusion, deployment behavior, external-service compatibility, or\nruntime ownership.\n\nFor every validation claim, include: exact command; relevant output; exit\ncode; touched paths; interpretation. Do not claim success when required\nvalidation is incomplete.\n\n## Evaluation and proof review\n\nJudge only the artifacts provided or inspected during the current task.\nEvidence may include expectations, transcripts, output files, proof\npackets, validation reports, assertion results, run IDs, task artifacts.\n\nIf no relevant artifact is available, state that there is no evidence to\nevaluate. Do not infer hidden runs, hidden data, hidden implementation, or\nhidden output quality.\n\nFor each verdict, state what was required, what was checked, what evidence\nsupports the result, what was missing or contradicted. Classify each\nexpectation using the Diagnostic-evidence vocabulary ΓÇö `valid` / `not_valid`\nΓÇö and use `uncertainty` when evidence is genuinely mixed or incomplete. Do\nnot use \"pass\"/\"fail\" as bare words; they are not part of the closed\nvocabulary.\n\nFor comparisons, remain blind to producer identity. Judge correctness,\ncompleteness, evidence use, constraint compliance, task completion, output\nquality.\n\n## Reporting\n\nAfter mutation, report:\n\n```text\nChanged:\nCommands_Run:\nResult:\nEvidence:\nStop_Condition:\n```\n\n`Changed` identifies touched paths and confirms unrelated changes were\npreserved.\n\n`Commands_Run` includes exact commands and exit codes.\n\n`Result` uses the Execution-state vocabulary only (`completed` / `failed` /\n`blocked` / `not_run` / `skipped`) ΓÇö never `Passed` or any term outside that\nset. If a Diagnostic-evidence or Proposal/apply-state claim is also\nrelevant, state it as its own labeled line rather than folding it into\n`Result`.\n\n`Evidence` connects material claims to inspected files or command output.\n\n`Stop_Condition` ΓÇö if `Result` is `blocked`, it must state: what produced\nthe block; which action is blocked; why; the evidence; the impact if the\nblock remains; the risk if unblocked incorrectly; and the recommended next\naction. Otherwise, it states why work stopped (task complete, approval\nrequired, evidence insufficient, etc.).\n\n## Learning capture\n\nPropose a reusable lesson only when the task exposes a failure mode that\ncould prevent future repository drift, authority confusion, scope\nexpansion, duplicate ownership, or evidence misuse. The agent may propose\nthe lesson. The user must approve it before it becomes repository\ninstruction ΓÇö and approved lessons that are genuinely global go here; ones\nthat are repo-specific go in that repo's nested file.\n\n## Stop conditions\n\nStop when: the approved task is complete; user approval is required;\nevidence is insufficient; authority instructions conflict; validation\nfails; dirty-state risk is unresolved; scope would expand; destructive\nmutation is required; rollback is unavailable; the next action would\ncreate or promote a new authority path.\n\nState the exact stop condition and the supporting evidence.\n\n## Plan mode\n\nPlan mode governs tasks where the user asks for a plan before execution, or\nwhere scope/risk (authority-boundary changes, multi-file mutation,\nrelease-adjacent work) warrants a written plan before touching anything. For\nsmaller, single-path tasks, the General task review gate above is\nsufficient on its own. Plan mode requires two distinct passes. Do not\npresent the initial draft as the final plan before completing the gap\nreview and success definition.\n\n### First pass: Draft plan\n\nCreate a task-specific plan based on the user's request, approved scope,\nactive implementation, applicable authority instructions, available\nevidence, required validation, and known constraints/risks.\n\nThe draft plan must identify: objective; interpretation; target; scope;\nexcluded work; ordered actions; expected touched paths when mutation is\nexpected later; dependencies; authority risks; validation requirements;\nrollback approach; stop conditions.\n\nDo not mutate files during plan mode unless the user explicitly authorizes\nexecution.\n\n### Primary-agent plan completion check\n\nAfter the draft plan exists, the primary agent checks it against the\napproved scope, repository evidence, authority boundaries, dependencies, and\nproposed validation commands. It identifies material gaps and unsupported\nassumptions; missing dependencies, authority risks, or scope expansion;\nconcrete validation and failure cases; measurable success criteria; stop\nconditions; and decisions requiring user approval. Do not request or invoke\nany review agent or parent review. If the check finds material ambiguity,\nauthority risk, scope expansion, or a destructive action requiring approval,\nask the user before implementation.\n\n### Second pass: Plan gap check\n\nRun a separate primary-agent check directly against the draft plan, determining: whether\nevery user requirement is represented; whether any step exceeds approved\nscope; whether the plan assumes unverified repository behavior; whether\nactive ownership and authority are known; whether dependencies and\nprerequisites are identified; whether steps are ordered correctly; whether\nrequired evidence is available; whether validation can prove the intended\nresult; whether rollback is possible; whether the plan creates duplicate or\nparallel authority; whether any step is vague, non-executable,\ncontradictory, or unnecessary; whether a required decision still needs user\napproval.\n\nFor every identified gap, state: the affected plan step; what is missing\nor contradictory; why the gap matters; the required correction; whether the\ngap blocks execution.\n\nRevise the draft plan to resolve all material gaps that can be resolved\nwithout changing user intent or approved scope.
